# Safety stock, lot sizing, detector sweep and alert routing - generated by `complete.py`, not hand-edited

## 1. Safety stock, with both sources of variation

```
SS = z * sqrt( L * sigma_d^2  +  d^2 * sigma_L^2 )
                \____________/    \_____________/
                 demand varies      supply varies
```

Both sides now use real inputs: demand spread from the Willems product demand standard deviations, lead-time spread from the part's Willems distribution plus its vendor's real SCMS lateness.

Across 209 purchased parts, **25% of the variance is supply-side on average** (39 parts are supply-dominated). The demand-only formula understates safety stock by only **1.29x**.

**This finding flipped.** The simulated version said 97% of the variance came from suppliers and the textbook formula understated stock 6.9x. The real data says the opposite: daily demand in this chain swings a lot (median coefficient of variation 0.95), while part lead times barely move (median CV 0.16; many parts have a single fixed lead time). The two-term formula is still the right one; it just matters little here.

| lead-time spread | empirical SS / parametric SS | parts |
|---|---:|---:|
| wide (P95/P50 >= 1.3) | 1.05x | 117 |
| narrow | 0.95x | 92 |

With lead-time spreads this small, the normal formula and the empirical quantile agree to within a few percent. **A bug the real data exposed:** the empirical version drew one day's demand and multiplied it by the lead time, so demand spread grew with L instead of sqrt(L). With the simulated demand (CV 0.25) this barely showed; with the real demand (CV about 0.95) it made the empirical safety stock 2.5-2.9x the formula. Fixed, with a test that a fixed lead time gives the formula's answer.

## 2. Lot sizing, MOQ and capacity

*MOQs are simulated (no public source) and supplier capacity is assumed.* Applying the minimums: **0 of 209 parts get raised to their minimum, forcing $0 of excess stock** at real unit costs. The real parts are cheap (median $0.48) and used in large volumes, so minimums rarely bind.


**Supplier capacity (assumed): 3 vendors over-committed**, total shortfall 4,552 units. Ordering earlier does not fix a capacity problem; a second source or a smaller order does.

## 3. The detector threshold sweep

Scored in the sandbox (real vendor lead times resampled, disruptions planted). A vendor needs 5+ orders in both windows to be judged.

| scale | judged | flagged | precision | recall | F1 |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1.05 | 23 | 15 | 0.27 | 0.67 | 0.38 |
| 1.10 | 23 | 10 | 0.40 | 0.67 | 0.50 |
| 1.15 | 23 | 7 | 0.43 | 0.50 | 0.46 |
| 1.25 | 23 | 5 | 0.40 | 0.33 | 0.36 |
| 1.40 | 23 | 4 | 0.50 | 0.33 | 0.40 |
| 1.60 | 23 | 4 | 0.50 | 0.33 | 0.40 |
| 2.00 | 23 | 2 | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.00 |

Best F1 at scale 1.10: precision 0.40, recall 0.67 against 6 planted disruptions.

**Which trigger earns its place:**

| trigger set | precision | recall |
|---|---:|---:|
| all three | 0.40 | 0.33 |
| without mean | 0.40 | 0.33 |
| without p95 | 0.40 | 0.33 |
| without variance | 0.50 | 0.33 |
- Removing **mean** changes nothing measurable here.
- Removing **p95** changes nothing measurable here.
- Removing **variance** keeps recall at 0.33 and raises precision 0.40 -> 0.50: it only adds false alarms.

## 4. Alert routing, severity tiers and SLAs

**209 alerts** (0 duplicates suppressed) across 209 purchased parts. Slack = projected run-out day (simulated stock and orders, real plan) minus the part's real lead time.

| severity | count | meaning | response SLA |
|---|---:|---|---|
| P1 | 0 | the line stops inside the lead time; no recovery by ordering | 4h |
| P2 | 0 | recoverable, but only if the order is placed now | 24h |
| P3 | 34 | comfortable slack; watch it | 72h |
| P4 | 175 | informational; batch into the weekly review | 168h |

82 parts run out inside the 13 weeks, the first on day 23. Every one of them can still be reordered at its normal lead time (3-55 days), so **none is P1**. The simulated version, with 14-75 day lead times, put 26 urgent items on one owner. The difference comes from real lead times being short; the stock rule is unchanged and simulated, so this says nothing about a real plant's stock position.

| owner | total | P1 | P2 | value at risk |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| BUYER | 209 | 0 | 0 | $14,730,015 |

Correlation between severity and supplier risk score: 0.69. Severity is about consequence and time, not supplier score.

## 5. Supplier distress proxy

Two observable signals: lead-time inflation (last year vs before) and a rise in the share of late lines. SCMS has no credit data, so the proxy is compared with the usual scorecard number, on-time vs scheduled.

| predictor of a planted disruption (sandbox) | AUROC |
|---|---:|
| distress proxy (lead inflation + late-rate rise) | **0.933** |
| on-time vs scheduled (the usual scorecard) | 0.962 |

6 planted disruptions across 26 vendors with enough history. Both separate them well, and the plain scorecard does slightly better. That result flatters the scorecard: in the sandbox a disruption delays the delivery but leaves the scheduled date where it was, so it shows up as lateness. In the real file 89% of lines land exactly on the scheduled date, which suggests the real date moves with the delay, and then on-time vs scheduled would see nothing. Lead-time inflation does not depend on the promise field at all.

On the **real** history the proxy ranks these vendors highest (no ground truth to check against):

| vendor | lead inflation | late-rate change | proxy |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| V03 S. BUYS WHOLESALER | 2.70x | -0.03 | 0.60 |
| V08 BIO-RAD LABORATORIES (FRANCE) | 1.82x | -0.16 | 0.49 |
| V25 GLAXOSMITHKLINE EXPORT LIMITED | 1.57x | +0.00 | 0.34 |
| V01 REINBOLD EXPORT IMPORT | 0.46x | +0.17 | 0.33 |
| V06 SHANGHAI KEHUA BIOENGINEERING  | 0.55x | +0.15 | 0.31 |
| V24 MICRO LABS LIMITED | 1.38x | +0.00 | 0.23 |

*still a proxy with stated weights; SCMS has no record of supplier failures, so the real-history ranking cannot be checked*
